# Custom Aluminium Extrusion: Die, Press Tonnage and Section Design

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/aluminium-extrusion-die-design/
Updated: 2026-11-15

To order a custom aluminium profile, the section is finalised in consultation with HyperFab’s engineering team, a dedicated extrusion die is built, and the profile is produced at the ordered tonnage. You bring the required tonnage and pay for the die. Die type, section size relative to press capacity and sound section design decide feasibility and cost.

## Short answer: how do you order a custom aluminium profile?

HyperFab specialises in aluminium extrusion, and aluminium only: other metals such as steel, brass and copper are not part of this service. The model is simple. You bring the required tonnage and pay for the die; section consultation, die making, profile production, quality control and delivery are handled by HyperFab’s engineering team.

This is a batch service, ordered by tonnage, meaning the weight of profile you order. The die cost and the profile price, which depends on alloy, weight and tonnage, are quoted separately. You will see both “aluminium” and “aluminum” in specifications; it is the same material and the same process.

## What is aluminium extrusion and how does it work?

Aluminium extrusion pushes a hot aluminium billet under press force through a steel die to make a long profile with a constant cross-section. The heated billet is loaded into the press container, the ram drives it towards the die, and the metal emerges through the die opening in the shape of the section. The profile is then cooled, straightened and cut to length, and where needed aged to reach its final temper.

Almost any section you can draw can be made with a dedicated die: solid, hollow, slotted, finned or with screw ports, which is why extrusion is the most economical way to make long, uniform aluminium parts. But extrusion dies are expensive, and a poorly designed section can lead to warped profiles, uneven surfaces or a broken die. That is why the section is reviewed before the die is made.

## Solid, semi-hollow and hollow extrusion dies: what is the difference?

The shape of the section decides the die type, not the buyer’s preference. The more fully enclosed voids a section has, the more complex and expensive the die becomes.

An extrusion die is designed and built for your section and produces only your profile, so it is part of your product’s tooling cost and the customer pays for it. It is quoted separately from the profile price. Agree how the die is stored and used for repeat orders with HyperFab when you receive the quotation.

| Die type | Suits which sections | How the die is built | Relative complexity and cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solid die | Sections with no enclosed void: angles, channels, flat bar and many heat sinks | A steel plate with an opening in the shape of the section | Simplest; lowest relative cost |
| Semi-hollow die | Sections that nearly enclose a void through a narrow gap, such as a deep slot or an open screw port | A die tongue forms the inner space and must survive the extrusion pressure | Sensitive to slot depth-to-width ratio; usually dearer than solid |
| Hollow die | Sections with one or more fully enclosed voids: tube, box section, housings and multi-cavity profiles | Two-part: a mandrel on bridges forms the void, and the split metal rejoins in a welding chamber | Most complex; highest relative cost |

## Press tonnage and the circumscribing circle: what limits section size?

In extrusion, “tonnage” can mean two things. Press tonnage is the force and capacity of the press that extrudes the profile; order tonnage is the weight of profile you buy. When HyperFab talks about the “required tonnage”, it means order tonnage. Whether your section suits the available press capacity is checked during section consultation.

The circumscribing circle is the smallest circle that fully encloses the cross-section. Each press, with its container and dies, can only extrude sections whose circle falls within its range, so a larger section needs a larger press.

Size is not the only limit. Walls that are very thin for the size of the section, several enclosed voids and harder-to-extrude alloys all need more pressure, so a section can fit the circle and still be difficult to extrude. If a section sits near the edge of the production range, splitting it into two profiles that snap or screw together is sometimes the more practical answer; that option is explored in consultation.

## Extrusion section design rules

These rules extend die life and lower the cost per kilo of profile. HyperFab’s engineering team checks all of them before the die is built and suggests changes where needed:

- Uniform wall thickness: large differences unbalance metal flow and warp the profile.
- Rounded corners: give sharp corners a small radius for longer die life and a better surface.
- Balanced section: symmetric, balanced sections extrude more stably and accurately.
- Avoid deep, narrow channels: they weaken the die tongue, so the depth-to-width ratio must be controlled.
- Enclose voids only where needed: if the function allows, opening one void can move the die from hollow to a simpler type.
- Tight tolerances on functional dimensions only; extruded profile tolerances are typically specified per EN 755.

## Which aluminium alloy and temper for extrusion? (6000 series)

Most extruded profiles are made from 6000-series alloys, with 6063 and 6061 the most widely used. 6063 extrudes more easily and gives a better surface, which suits architectural and decorative profiles, thin and intricate sections, and parts that will be anodized. 6061 is stronger and is chosen for structural work, but it is harder to extrude, and thin, complex sections are more demanding in it.

The temper is part of the profile specification too and is usually written on the drawing with a designation such as T5 or T6. If you know the alloy and temper, put them on the drawing; if not, describe the use, the loads and the final finish and the engineering team will advise. The alloy also affects the profile price.

An extruded profile is rarely the finished product. Anodizing, powder coating, machining, punching and aluminium welding are also available at HyperFab.

## How to order a custom aluminium profile, and what drives the price

Ordering takes five steps: send the section drawing, a DXF or even a sketch with the profile’s use; section consultation and tonnage advice; a quotation with die cost and profile price shown separately; die making and a sample profile for your approval; and finally production at the ordered tonnage, inspection and delivery. The price comes from the factors below, and no meaningful figure can be given before the section has been reviewed.

- Die type and complexity: solid, semi-hollow or hollow.
- Section size and its circumscribing circle relative to the production range.
- Section weight and wall thickness.
- Alloy and temper.
- Order tonnage.
- Tolerances and surface requirements.
- Follow-on work such as anodizing, powder coating and machining.

For consultation and an exact quote, call HyperFab’s industrial projects specialist on 09962233898 (+98 996 223 3898) or send the section drawing on Bale.

## FAQ

### Who owns the extrusion die?

The customer pays for the dedicated die, and it is built only for that customer’s section. Agree ownership, storage and use of the die for later orders with HyperFab when you receive the quotation.

### Is there a minimum order for aluminium extrusion?

HyperFab takes extrusion orders by tonnage. The right tonnage depends on the size and weight of the section and is advised after consultation.

### Does HyperFab extrude metals other than aluminium?

No. In extrusion, HyperFab works with aluminium only. If you need brass or steel parts, HyperFab’s batch CNC turning may suit, depending on the part.

### What drawing or file do you need?

A section drawing, a DXF or even a hand sketch, together with the profile’s use, is enough to start. Add the alloy, temper and final finish if you know them; you can also send the details by phone or on Bale.

# Anodizing vs Electroplating vs Chromate Conversion: Which Finish?

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/anodizing-vs-plating-vs-chromate/
Updated: 2026-11-15

Anodizing grows a hard, insulating oxide out of the aluminium itself. Chromate conversion (Alodine) forms a very thin, conductive film on aluminium. Electroplating deposits a different metal, such as silver or gold, onto brass and other metals. Start with the base metal, then decide whether conductivity, wear resistance or appearance matters most for the part.

## Anodizing vs plating vs chromate at a glance

These three finishes get mixed up because they all count as surface treatment, but they work in completely different ways. Anodizing and chromate conversion act on the aluminium itself and turn its surface into a new compound; electroplating deposits a layer of another metal on top of the part. That difference drives everything else: conductivity, appearance and even whether the part's dimensions change.

| Finish | Base metal | How it forms | Surface conductivity | Appearance | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anodizing | Aluminium | Controlled electrochemical oxidation of the aluminium in an electrolyte bath | Insulating | Matt to satin; natural, black or dyed colours | Device housings, profiles, industrial and decorative parts |
| Chromate (Alodine) | Aluminium | Chemical reaction with a conversion solution, no current | Conductive | Clear or faint yellow-gold | Electronic parts, enclosures, paint base |
| Silver plating | Brass, copper and other metals | Silver electro-deposited from a plating bath | Highest of any metal | Bright white silver; tarnishes over time | Contacts, connectors, busbars, RF parts, decorative items |
| Gold plating | Brass, copper and other metals | Gold electro-deposited, usually over an underlayer | Conductive, stable contact resistance | Gold; does not oxidise | Connectors and electronics, luxury hardware, decorative items |

## What is aluminium anodizing and what colours are available?

Anodizing (also spelled anodising) is an electrochemical process in which the aluminium part is made the anode of a circuit, so the thin natural oxide on its surface is thickened in a controlled way. The layer is not paint sitting on the metal: it grows out of the aluminium, which is why it does not flake. The result is a harder surface with better corrosion and wear resistance.

Anodizing is for aluminium, and the alloy affects the result: 6000-series extrusion alloys usually anodize evenly, while high-copper and casting alloys can come out duller and patchier.

A key advantage of anodizing is that it can be coloured. The fresh oxide is porous and absorbs dye before sealing; sealing then locks the colour inside the layer. The surface finish beforehand matters as much as the dye: a bead-blasted part comes out evenly matt, a polished one brighter. Common options:

- Natural or clear: keeps the silver look of the aluminium.
- Black: common on device housings, optical parts and tools.
- Dyed colours such as gold, red or blue: for cosmetic and decorative parts.

## What is chromate conversion (Alodine) and why does it stay conductive?

Chromate conversion coating, widely known by the trade name Alodine, is a conversion coating: the aluminium surface reacts with a chemical solution and forms a very thin film, with no electric current and no other metal deposited. The film is so thin that part dimensions are effectively unchanged and the surface stays electrically conductive.

That is what makes chromate the right call for electronic parts and enclosures that must be grounded or provide EMI shielding, where an insulating anodized layer gets in the way. Chromate is also a good paint base: applied before powder coating on aluminium, it improves adhesion.

Know its limits, though. The film is soft and thin and does not resist wear and scratching the way anodizing does. Chromate is typically specified per MIL-DTL-5541, which has separate classes for maximum corrosion protection and for low electrical resistance. If your product has to comply with restrictions on hexavalent chromium, say so when you order.

## Why plate brass with silver or gold?

Brass is a common choice for electrical parts and fittings because it machines easily and conducts reasonably well. But brass oxidises and dulls in air, and its contact resistance creeps up over time. HyperFab carries out silver and gold plating on brass and other metals for production runs, and it pairs naturally with batch CNC turning of brass parts: the turned part comes back plated and ready to fit.

Which one to choose depends on use, environment and budget. Silver costs less but tarnishes; gold costs more but does not oxidise. Gold on brass is usually applied over an underlayer such as nickel, which stops the base metal from migrating into the gold. The three main reasons to plate brass:

- Conductivity: silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any metal, so it is used on busbars, high-current contacts and RF parts.
- Reliable contact: gold does not oxidise, so its contact resistance stays stable over time; the choice for signal connectors and electronics.
- Appearance: a bright silver or gold look for hardware, statuettes, badges and corporate gifts.

## Which finish suits my part? Choosing by base metal and use

Fix the base metal first, then the part's main requirement. If you are still unsure, describe the part's use and environment over the phone:

- Aluminium part that needs wear and corrosion resistance, in black or a colour: anodizing.
- Aluminium part that must stay conductive, be grounded or be painted later: chromate (Alodine).
- Aluminium part that needs both: anodizing with the contact areas masked, or chromate all over, depending on whether wear or conductivity matters more.
- Brass or copper contacts, busbars or connectors carrying high current: silver plating.
- Signal connectors, or contacts that must stay reliable in humid conditions: gold plating.
- Steel parts: aluminium anodizing and chromate do not apply; powder coating is the usual choice for protection and appearance.

## How to prepare drawings for plating and anodizing (masking)

Most problems in batch finishing start with an ambiguous drawing. Masking means temporarily covering part of the component with plugs, tape or a special lacquer so the finish does not reach it. It is manual work and adds cost, so mask only what really needs it. When parts are finished on racks, the contact point with the rack is usually left bare; mark a hidden surface for it. Parts should also arrive free of burrs, oil and swarf, because a finish does not hide surface defects and often makes them more visible.

Before you send the drawing, make sure it or the order notes state:

- The exact material and alloy, for example the brass grade or aluminium alloy.
- The finish, colour and gloss, and any standard it is specified to (for example ISO 7599 for anodizing).
- Surfaces that must stay uncoated: threads, precision bores, mating faces and grounding points.
- Whether the drawing dimensions apply before or after finishing, especially for threads and fits.

## What affects the cost of plating, anodizing and chromate?

Each project is quoted after the part has been reviewed. The main factors are:

- Finish type: gold plating costs more than silver, anodizing or chromate because of the precious metal.
- The coating thickness called out on the drawing and any standard requirements.
- Part size, surface area and shape, and how many parts fit on a rack or in a tank at once.
- Masking, and how many surfaces must stay uncoated.
- Anodizing colour and any requirement for colour matching between batches.
- The condition of the parts and the preparation needed before finishing.
- Quantity: the service is for production runs, and one-off parts are accepted only rarely.

For an exact quote, have the part material, the finish, a drawing or sample and the quantity ready, and call 09962233898.

## FAQ

### Can steel be anodized?

No. In industry, anodizing is mainly used on aluminium and a few other light metals; steel does not form a protective, adherent oxide, and its oxide is simply rust. HyperFab anodizes aluminium only, and powder coating is the usual finish for steel parts.

### Is chromate conversion conductive?

Yes. The chromate (Alodine) film is thin enough that the aluminium surface stays electrically conductive. That is why it is chosen for enclosures and parts that must be grounded, whereas anodizing insulates.

### Does anodizing change part dimensions?

Yes, slightly. Part of the anodic layer penetrates into the metal and part builds up on the surface, so outside dimensions grow a little and holes shrink a little. For threads and precision fits, either mask those areas or state on the drawing that dimensions apply after finishing.

### Why plate brass with silver?

Bare brass oxidises in air and its contact resistance rises. Silver plating gives it the highest conductivity of any metal and a bright white finish, which suits contacts, busbars and connectors. Silver tarnishes over time, so where stable contact over the long term is critical, gold is the better choice.

# Batch CNC Turning of Brass Fittings: What Drives the Price

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/brass-cnc-turning-batch/
Updated: 2026-11-15

The price of batch-turned brass fittings depends on the brass alloy and bar size, the part's complexity (threads, holes and secondary operations), the tolerances on fit and sealing surfaces, the quantity, and any finish such as plating. Machine setup is spread across the whole run, which is why HyperFab takes this work as production runs.

## Where does the cost of a batch-turned brass fitting come from?

Every turned brass fitting is priced from a handful of components: the brass itself, machine time per part, setup (programming, tooling, workholding and first-article approval), secondary operations such as threading and knurling, dimensional inspection, and any final finish. How much each one weighs depends on the design and the quantity.

At low quantities, setup is a large share of each part's price. As the run grows, that share shrinks and machine time and material take over. That is why, in batch work, designing the part to be easier to make, for example dropping operations that add nothing or choosing a sensible bar diameter, is where most of the savings are.

## Why are fittings made from brass? Brass vs steel vs stainless

Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is the standard material for pipe fittings, valves, nozzles, bushings and mating parts. There are three main reasons: short chips and fast, clean cutting; good corrosion resistance in water and ordinary atmospheres; and a surface that takes silver and gold plating well. It also conducts electricity well, so it shows up in connectors and electrical parts.

Carbon steel, by contrast, is stronger and cheaper as raw material but rusts without a coating, while stainless steel resists corrosion very well but cuts harder and slower. The table compares the three qualitatively for turned fittings.

| Property | Brass | Carbon steel | Stainless steel |
|---|---|---|---|
| Machinability | Very good, short chips | Good | Fair to difficult, more tool wear |
| Cycle time per part | Short | Medium | Long |
| Corrosion resistance | Good in water and normal atmospheres | Poor without a coating | Very good |
| Silver and gold plating | Good substrate | Possible, with more preparation | Possible, with special preparation |
| Strength | Moderate | High | High |
| Material cost (relative) | Higher than carbon steel | Low | Higher than carbon steel |
| Typical uses | Plumbing and gas fittings, nozzles, connectors, mating parts | Shafts, pins, loaded parts | Sanitary, food, medical and marine fittings |

## Why is brass fitting turning done in batches only?

A lot happens before the first acceptable part comes off the machine: drawing review, programming, choosing and setting tools, workholding, making the first article, then measuring and adjusting until it is approved. That cost is roughly the same whether you need one part or a thousand.

In a production run, that cost is spread over the whole batch and the price per part stays reasonable. That is why HyperFab's batch CNC turning service is for production runs: one-off parts are accepted only rarely, and a suitable quantity is recommended after reviewing the project. For single parts and prototypes, CNC machining on hyperfab.ir is the better fit.

In batch work, the real challenge is not making one good part. It is making hundreds or thousands of fittings that are all exactly as good as the approved sample. You approve the first article before the run starts, and dimensions are checked during production and again before delivery.

## Cheap turner or expensive turner: what are you actually paying for?

Two quotes for the same drawing can be far apart. Part of the gap is work that the cheaper quote simply leaves out: nobody checks before cutting which face seals, which diameter has to mate with another part, or which thread needs gauging. The result tends to show up at assembly as a leak, a thread that will not tighten properly, or a part that will not seat. With brass fittings, a bad batch usually costs more than the original price difference, because the defect often appears only after plating and assembly.

Precision beyond what the part needs is a cost too. HyperFab matches the production method and precision level to each part's requirements: no more expensive than needed, never below requirements. In a sound quote, this is what you are buying:

- Drawing engineering before production: identifying fit surfaces, critical diameters, concentricity and sealing faces.
- A technical briefing for the machinist, so they know where each part needs which accuracy and how it will be measured.
- First-article approval before the production run starts.
- Dimensional inspection during production and before delivery.
- Suitable packing, so threads and fit surfaces arrive undamaged.

## How do threads, knurling and secondary operations affect price?

Few brass fittings are a plain turned profile. Internal and external threads, knurling for hand grip, cross holes, wrench flats or hexes, O-ring grooves and deburring each add time, and some add a separate operation.

The earlier and more completely these are defined on the drawing, the more accurate the quote, and the less chance of unplanned costs later.

- Threads: state the thread type and standard (tapered or parallel pipe thread, metric or inch) and its class precisely; gauged threads take longer to inspect.
- Knurling: specify the pattern (straight or diamond) and where it runs on the part.
- Hexes and flats: starting from hexagonal bar avoids a separate milling step and brings cost down.
- Cross holes and milling: anything the lathe cannot do in the same setup may need re-clamping and more time.
- Deburring and cleaning: on water and gas fittings and on parts going for plating, leftover burrs and oil cause trouble.

## Can brass parts be plated after turning?

Yes. Brass is a good base for silver and gold plating, and you can hand the plating to HyperFab in the same project and receive the part turned, plated and ready to use. Silver plating gives the highest electrical conductivity and is common on contacts and connectors; gold does not oxidise and keeps a stable contact resistance.

If a part will be plated, plan for it from the start. Plating builds a layer on the surface, so precision threads and fit surfaces have to be designed and turned with that in mind. Mark any surfaces that must stay unplated on the drawing. Turned finish and deburring also show directly in the final appearance, because plating does not hide surface defects.

Plating, like turning, is a batch service. If the part needs a decorative or electrical finish, or no finish at all, say so in the enquiry so it is reflected in the quote.

## What to send for a quote, and what the price depends on

A dimensioned drawing with tolerances is the key document. Send a 3D model (a STEP file, for example) if you have one, but it does not replace the drawing. The final price depends on:

- The brass alloy and the bar size and shape (round or hexagonal)
- Part complexity: the number of steps, threads, holes and secondary operations
- Tolerances, fit surfaces and sealing faces
- Quantity and whether the order repeats
- Finish: silver plating, gold plating or none
- Special inspection, such as thread gauging or a dimensional report
- Packing requirements

Have this information ready and call 09962233898 for an exact quote. HyperFab is based in Tehran and recommends a price and a suitable quantity after reviewing the drawing.

## FAQ

### Do you accept single pieces?

HyperFab's batch CNC turning service is for production runs; one-off parts are accepted only rarely, and a suitable quantity is recommended after reviewing the project. For single parts and prototypes, see CNC machining on hyperfab.ir.

### Can parts be plated after turning?

Yes. Silver and gold plating on brass parts is available at HyperFab, and the finished part is delivered. If plating is needed, mention it up front so threads and fit surfaces are reviewed with the coating in mind.

### What file do you need for a quote?

A dimensioned drawing with tolerances, thread specifications, the material and the quantity. A 3D model such as a STEP file helps but does not replace the drawing. If you have no drawing, a sample part or a phone description can be a starting point.

### Which brass alloy should I use for fittings?

Turned fittings are usually made from free-cutting (leaded) brass, which breaks into short chips and machines quickly. Parts in contact with drinking water may need a low-lead or lead-free brass under the product standard. The designer or the product standard sets the alloy, and it can be discussed during the drawing review.

# From Design to Production: Injection Mould Making Step by Step

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/injection-mould-making-steps/
Updated: 2026-11-15

An injection moulding project runs from part design for moulding, through mould design and steel selection, CNC machining, EDM and polishing, to trial shots, corrections and finally production. Most of the risk sits in the early stages, so every change made before steel is cut costs far less than one made afterwards.

## What are the stages of injection mould making?

Mould making (mold making in US spelling) and injection moulding are two halves of one project. First a steel mould is built that carries the shape of the part; then an injection moulding machine fills it with molten polymer, shot after shot. Much of the final part quality is decided on the day the part design and mould design are frozen.

At HyperFab the route starts with a mouldability review of the design. The mould is then designed and built, sampling and correction continue until you approve the part, and production follows with quality control.

| Stage | What happens | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Design for moulding | Review of draft, wall thickness, ribs, undercuts and material | Corrected, mouldable 3D model |
| Mould design | Parting line, cavity count, runner and gate, cooling and ejection | Mould drawings and steel selection |
| Mould build | CNC machining, EDM, polishing and assembly | Mould ready for trials |
| Trial shots (T0, T1) | Test moulding, measurement and mould corrections | Approved sample |
| Production | Moulding runs on locked settings with quality checks | Parts ready for delivery |

## Designing a part for injection moulding: draft, wall thickness and ribs

A design that prints or machines well is not necessarily mouldable. The first rule is draft: walls parallel to the direction the mould opens need a slight taper so the part releases without scuffing or sticking. The right amount depends on the material, wall depth and surface texture, and is set during the design review.

The second rule is uniform wall thickness. Polymer shrinks as it cools, and thick sections cool last, which causes warping, sink marks and internal voids. Instead of thick walls, use ribs for stiffness and bosses for screw points. A rib should be thinner than the wall it supports so it does not leave a mark on the opposite face.

Undercuts, features that stop the part coming straight out of the mould, need slides or lifters and make the mould more expensive; a small design change can often remove them. Sharp internal corners are better rounded, which helps material flow and reduces stress concentration. Tolerances should be realistic for the chosen material and its shrinkage.

## Mould design and choosing the mould steel

Mould design settles a few key questions: where the parting line goes, how many cavities the mould has, where and through what kind of runner (cold or hot runner) the material enters, how the cooling channels cool the part evenly, and where the ejector pins sit. Gate position directly affects the part’s appearance, weld lines and warpage.

Shrinkage is built into the cavity dimensions: the cavity is cut slightly larger than the finished part, by an amount that depends on the material. That is why the material must be fixed before the mould is built. Switching later, say from polyethylene to ABS, may mean modifying the mould.

Steel choice depends on volume, polymer and the finish required. Pre-hardened mould steels suit many medium-volume projects and are easier to machine. For very high volumes or abrasive materials such as glass-filled grades, a hardened tool steel lasts longer, and stainless mould steel is used for corrosive polymers or high-gloss finishes.

## Building the mould: CNC machining, EDM and polishing

Most of the cavity and core material is removed by CNC milling. Where a cutter cannot reach, such as deep narrow ribs, sharp internal corners and fine detail, the shape is made by spark erosion, or electrical discharge machining (EDM): a graphite or copper electrode copies its form into the steel. Wire EDM is also used for precise holes and inserts.

After machining, the cavity surfaces are polished. The level of polish depends on the part: a hidden industrial part needs only a basic finish, while a cosmetic or transparent part needs a high gloss. If a textured surface is required, say so at the start, because texture affects the draft the part needs. Finally the slides, ejector pins and cooling circuit are assembled and the mould is ready for trials.

## What are T0 and T1 trial shots, and what gets corrected?

The first test moulding with a new tool is usually called T0. Its purpose is to find problems, not to produce finished parts. The trial checks whether the cavity fills completely or gives short shots, whether flash appears on the parting line, and looks for sink marks, warpage, ejector marks and how easily the part releases. Samples are measured and compared with the drawing.

Some issues are solved by adjusting process settings such as pressure, speed and cooling time; others need steel to be modified. Toolmakers often cut critical dimensions steel-safe, leaving a little extra metal, because removing steel is easier than adding it. After corrections, the next trial (T1, and further rounds if needed) brings the part into line with the drawing.

At HyperFab, samples are moulded once the mould is built, and production starts only after you approve them.

## How does the production run work?

Once a sample is approved, the process settings are locked and recorded so that every production run produces the same part. Raw material is prepared before moulding; some polymers, such as nylon and polycarbonate, absorb moisture and are dried first. During production, parts are checked at intervals for dimensions and appearance, and the mould itself needs care: cleaning, lubricating the slides and checking the cooling circuit.

HyperFab carries out production runs in polyethylene, polypropylene, ABS, nylon and engineering thermoplastics such as polycarbonate and acetal. Its team has taken four polyethylene injection moulds from build supervision to commissioning, and more than 80,000 parts have been produced with them. Orders for this service are arranged by phone.

## What drives the cost of mould making and injection moulding?

An injection project is priced in two parts, quoted separately: a one-off mould cost and a cost per shot in production. The main drivers are:

- Part size and complexity, and therefore mould size.
- Number of cavities.
- Undercuts and the slides or lifters they require.
- Required surface finish, polish or texture.
- Mould steel and runner type (cold or hot runner).
- Number of trial rounds and design changes after the build has started.
- Per shot: polymer type, grade and colour, part weight, cycle time and run quantity.

For an exact quote, have your 3D file, drawing or sample part ready and call 09962233898. After a mouldability review, HyperFab quotes the mould cost and the cost per shot separately. If you are not yet sure about volumes, you can make a first prototype with 3D printing on hyperfab.ir.

## FAQ

### What drives mould cost?

The main factors are part size and complexity, the number of cavities, undercuts and slides, surface finish and the mould steel. HyperFab quotes the mould separately from the cost per shot after reviewing the design.

### How many cavities do I need?

It depends on total volume, part size, the injection machine’s capacity and your budget. A single-cavity mould is cheaper to build but keeps the cost per part higher; a multi-cavity mould is the reverse. The right number is recommended during the design review, based on your expected volumes.

### Who owns the mould?

By common practice, a mould the customer has paid for normally belongs to the customer. Even so, ownership, storage location, maintenance responsibility and the right to move the mould should be set out in writing in the agreement. Raise these points with HyperFab when you request a quote.

### Can a 3D-printed prototype come first?

Yes, and it is a good idea. An FDM 3D print lets you check form, dimensions and assembly on a real part, and you can price it online at hyperfab.ir. Keep in mind that a printed part does not have the mechanical properties or surface of a moulded one, so it mainly confirms geometry.

# MO40 vs CK45 Steel for Gauges and Turned Parts

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/mo40-vs-ck45-steel/
Updated: 2026-11-15

MO40 (42CrMo4, 1.7225) is a chromium-molybdenum alloy steel; CK45 (C45E, 1.1191) is a plain medium-carbon steel. MO40 hardens deeper and more evenly and stays tougher, so it suits heavily used gauges and loaded parts. CK45 costs less and responds well to induction hardening, which makes it the economical choice for simple gauges and general turned parts.

## MO40 vs CK45 at a glance

The short answer: MO40 is a chromium-molybdenum alloy steel, CK45 is a plain medium-carbon steel. Their carbon content is similar, so the surface hardness each reaches after quenching is not very different. What separates them is how deep and how evenly they harden, how tough they are after heat treatment, and what they cost.

If a part works under load, impact or constant wear, or has a thick section that must harden through to the core, MO40 is the safer pick. If the part is simple, lightly loaded, or only needs a hard working surface, CK45 does the job for less money. The table compares the two qualitatively.

| Property | MO40 (42CrMo4) | CK45 (C45E) |
|---|---|---|
| Steel type | Low-alloy chromium-molybdenum steel | Plain medium-carbon steel |
| Hardenability (depth of hardening) | High; thicker sections harden through to the core | Low; thick sections mainly harden at the surface |
| Toughness after heat treatment | High | Moderate |
| Machinability | Good; harder on tools when bought quenched and tempered | Good and predictable, especially when normalised |
| Typical uses | Loaded and impact-loaded shafts and parts, heavily used gauges | General shafts and pins, machine parts, simple gauges |
| Relative cost | Higher | Lower |

## What are the equivalents of MO40 and CK45, and how does their composition differ?

MO40 is the name the Iranian market uses for 42CrMo4, material number 1.7225. It is a medium-carbon steel with chromium and molybdenum added, and those two elements are what raise its hardenability and toughness. The closest American equivalent is AISI 4140.

CK45 is the old German DIN name for the steel now designated C45E, material number 1.1191. It is a plain medium-carbon steel with no significant alloying. The "k" in the old name refers to tighter control of impurities such as phosphorus and sulphur. Close equivalents are C45 and AISI 1045.

Equivalents are close, not identical. Element ranges differ slightly between standards, and bar sold under one name in the market is not always exactly that grade. For gauges and other critical parts, ask for the mill certificate or have the material checked by analysis.

## Which one hardens better? MO40 vs CK45 heat treatment

It helps to separate hardness from hardenability. Hardness is how hard the surface gets after quenching, and it depends mostly on carbon content, which is similar in these two steels. Hardenability is how deep that hardness reaches below the surface, and this is where the chromium and molybdenum in MO40 make the difference.

MO40 hardens to a good depth even with a milder quench. That makes it well suited to through-hardening followed by tempering (quench and temper), after which it is both strong and tough. It is also widely sold already quenched and tempered. CK45 needs a more severe quench to harden, which raises the risk of distortion and cracking, and in thick sections it effectively hardens only in an outer layer.

That is why CK45 is the usual candidate for surface hardening: induction or flame hardening puts a hard skin on the working surface while the core stays tough. MO40 can be surface hardened or nitrided too, when a wear-resistant surface over a strong core is needed.

- Through-hardening and tempering: the natural route for MO40, especially in thick sections.
- Induction or flame hardening: the common route for CK45 shafts, pins and wear surfaces.
- Nitriding: an option for MO40 when a hard surface is needed with minimal dimensional change.
- Either way: the part is turned before heat treatment with enough stock left for final grinding.

## Is MO40 or CK45 easier to machine?

In the normalised or annealed condition both steels machine well, and CK45 is usually a little easier and cheaper to turn. When MO40 is bought quenched and tempered it is stronger, tools wear faster and cutting has to slow down, which feeds straight into machine time and cost per part.

The order of operations matters as much as the grade. A part that will be hardened is typically rough-turned first, stress relieved if needed, then heat treated, and finally ground or finished on the precision surfaces. If that sequence is not stated on the drawing or in the enquiry, a part turned accurately in the soft state can distort in heat treatment and end up out of tolerance.

In HyperFab's batch CNC turning, each part's critical points are engineered and briefed to the machinist before production: fit surfaces, critical diameters, concentricity and the grinding allowance. That keeps the production route matched to the material and to what the part actually has to do.

## Which steel is better for gauges, MO40 or CK45?

A gauge is the precision reference of a production line, and any error in it passes straight into the product. Three things drive the material choice: wear resistance on the measuring surfaces, dimensional stability over time, and the ability to survive knocks and drops on the shop floor.

Gauges are usually heat treated after turning, and their measuring surfaces are ground so they end up both hard and accurate. Because MO40 hardens deeper and more evenly and moves less in heat treatment, it is the safer choice for heavily used gauges, thick-section gauges, and gauges with thin lips or slender features. CK45 is an economical choice for simple, lightly used gauges, or for gauges where only the working surface is induction hardened.

For master gauges or gauges facing very severe wear, designers often move to tool steels instead. HyperFab has produced batch gauge parts in both MO40 and CK45, and those parts were approved by the customers. The final material call belongs to the gauge designer, and it can be discussed during the drawing review.

## What drives the cost of an MO40 or CK45 turned part?

Material is where the price starts, but not where it ends. These factors carry the most weight:

- Grade and bar diameter: MO40 costs more than CK45, and unusual diameters can be more expensive to source.
- Supply condition: machining quenched-and-tempered MO40 takes more machine time and tooling.
- Heat treatment and grinding: the hardening method (through, induction or nitriding) and how many surfaces need grinding.
- Tolerances and surface finish: more fit surfaces and critical diameters mean more time and inspection. General tolerances are typically specified per ISO 2768 on the drawing.
- Part complexity: the number of steps, grooves, threads and secondary operations.
- Quantity: setup and first-article approval are spread over more parts.

For an exact quote, prepare a dimensioned drawing with tolerances, the material, the heat treatment you need and the quantity, and call 09962233898. HyperFab's CNC turning service is for production runs, and a first article is approved by you before the run starts.

## FAQ

### What is MO40's equivalent grade?

MO40 is 42CrMo4, material number 1.7225, and its closest American equivalent is AISI 4140. These equivalents are close rather than identical, so check the mill certificate for critical parts.

### Which gets harder after heat treatment, MO40 or CK45?

Their surface hardness after quenching is similar, because their carbon content is similar. The difference is depth: MO40 hardens deeper and more evenly and is tougher after tempering, while CK45 in thick sections hardens mainly at the surface.

### Can CK45 be induction hardened?

Yes, and it is one of CK45's most common uses. Induction hardening gives a shaft, pin or gauge a hard working surface while the core stays tough. Precision surfaces are usually ground after hardening.

### Which lasts longer as a gauge, MO40 or CK45?

Under the same working conditions and with proper heat treatment, an MO40 gauge usually holds its dimensions better and resists wear and impact longer. For a lightly used gauge, hardened CK45 is often enough and costs less. The quality of the heat treatment and grinding matters as much as the grade.

# Powder Coating: Process, Powder Types and Finish Choices

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/powder-coating-process-finishes/
Updated: 2026-11-15

Powder coating is a dry powder that is electrostatically charged, sprayed onto a metal part and melted and cured in an oven into a hard, even layer. How well it performs depends on surface preparation, the powder chemistry (epoxy, polyester or hybrid) and a correct cure, while gloss and texture should be chosen to suit the part's use.

## Powder types: epoxy, polyester or hybrid?

Before you pick a colour or texture, the most important decision is the resin the powder is based on, because it decides how the coating behaves outdoors and in sunlight.

The rule of thumb is simple: parts that see sunlight need polyester; where chemical resistance and adhesion indoors matter most, epoxy; and for most indoor parts where looks matter, a hybrid. For harsher conditions, such as coastal sites, the preparation and powder should be agreed together from the start.

| Powder | Indoor or outdoor | UV resistance | Strength | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Epoxy | Indoor | Poor; chalks and fades in sunlight | Strong adhesion, chemical and corrosion resistance | Parts inside machines, sheltered industrial equipment, primer coats |
| Polyester | Outdoor and indoor | Good; holds colour and gloss outdoors | Weather resistance | Outdoor structures and facades, aluminium profiles, outdoor furniture, vehicle parts |
| Epoxy-polyester hybrid | Indoor | Moderate; not for direct sun | Good looks, balanced properties and cost | Appliances, office furniture, indoor shelving and electrical cabinets |

## Why is surface preparation the most important step?

Powder only bonds well to a clean, properly prepared surface. Most failures that show up months later as flaking or rust creeping under the coating trace back to poor preparation, not to the powder itself.

Welded parts need extra care: spatter, slag, sharp edges and open seams must be dealt with before coating, because the powder will not hide them. Castings and galvanized parts can also release gas during curing and need specific preparation. Depending on the material and its condition, preparation may include:

- Degreasing to remove cutting oil, grease and handling marks.
- Removing rust, mill scale or oxide, mechanically by abrasive blasting or chemically.
- A conversion coating for better adhesion and corrosion resistance: phosphating on steel, and chromate (Alodine) or its alternatives on aluminium.
- Thorough rinsing and drying, because trapped moisture ends up sealed under the powder.

## How is powder applied and cured?

After preparation, parts are hung on hooks or racks in a spray booth. The electrostatic gun charges the powder particles and the grounded part attracts them, which is why powder also wraps around edges and onto the back of the part. Overspray is usually collected and reused.

The part then goes into the oven. The powder melts, flows out over the surface and then cures chemically into a hard, continuous film. The cure schedule is set by the powder manufacturer and has to account for the metal thickness, since heavy parts take longer to reach temperature.

Two design points follow from this. First, the part must survive the oven, so plastic and rubber parts, seals and bonded assemblies have to be removed beforehand. Second, the hanging point stays uncoated, so plan a hole or tab for it. Threads, precision bores and grounding points are usually masked with heat-resistant plugs or tape.

## Gloss, matte, texture or pearl: choosing a finish and RAL colour

Specify colour by its standard RAL code rather than a description or photo, since screens and prints never show colour accurately. Pearl and metallic powders can vary slightly between powder batches; if parts will sit side by side, coat them in one order and approve a reference sample. Some metallic powders need a clear topcoat for outdoor use.

Once the powder type is settled, gloss and texture set the final look:

- Gloss: makes colours look richer and is easy to clean, but shows surface unevenness and scratches more.
- Satin and matte: a calmer, more industrial look that hides minor surface flaws better.
- Texture and wrinkle: a rough surface that hides fingerprints and scratches; good for housings and high-touch parts.
- Hammer: looks like hammered metal and hides imperfections; common on cabinets, tools and machinery.
- Pearl and metallic: metallic or pearlescent particles give a lustrous sheen for cosmetic parts and premium products.

## Common powder coating defects and how to prevent them

Most powder coating defects can be prevented, and the cause is usually preparation, part design or curing. Adhesion is typically checked with a cross-cut test per ISO 2409. The usual suspects:

- Flaking and poor adhesion: usually inadequate degreasing or preparation.
- Pinholes and blisters (outgassing): gas escaping from castings, galvanized steel or weld seams during curing; reduced by proper preparation and pre-heating.
- Orange peel: a wavy surface caused by the wrong film build or curing conditions.
- Thin coverage in inside corners: the Faraday cage effect keeps powder out of deep recesses; more open corners in the design help.
- Craters: contamination with oil or silicone; solved by cleaning and keeping silicone sprays away from parts before coating.
- Yellowing or fading: over-curing, or using epoxy powder outdoors.
- Rust starting at edges: powder builds thin on sharp edges, so chamfer or round them before coating.

## Powder coating vs liquid paint: what is the difference?

Powder coating builds a thicker, harder film than liquid paint in a single coat and stands up better to impact, scratches and corrosion. It contains no solvent, does not run, and overspray can be recovered. It is also more consistent across a batch, because film build and appearance repeat from part to part.

Liquid paint is still the better choice in a few cases: parts that cannot take oven heat, such as plastics and wood; structures larger than the oven or that must be painted on site; and local touch-ups. Repairing damaged powder coating is also harder, and is usually done with a matching liquid paint.

## What affects the cost of powder coating?

Each order is quoted after the parts have been reviewed. The main factors are:

- Part size and total surface area, and how many parts fit in the booth and oven at once.
- Weight and metal thickness, which set how long the part takes to reach curing temperature.
- Powder type (epoxy, polyester or hybrid) and special effects such as pearl, metallic or hammer.
- Preparation required: simple degreasing, abrasive blasting, phosphating or chromate.
- Masking of threads, holes and uncoated surfaces.
- Uncommon colours and colour changes between orders.
- Quantity: HyperFab's powder coating service is for production runs, and one-off parts are accepted only rarely.

For an exact quote, have the part size and material, the powder type and colour and the quantity ready, or send a sample, and call 09962233898.

## FAQ

### Powder coating or liquid paint?

For batch metal parts that can take oven heat, powder coating is usually more durable and more consistent. Liquid paint is better suited to heat-sensitive parts, very large structures, on-site painting and touch-ups.

### Is powder coating suitable for outdoor use?

Yes, with the right powder. Polyester powders are made for outdoor exposure and sunlight, while epoxy and hybrid powders chalk and fade in the sun. Good surface preparation matters just as much for outdoor durability.

### Can aluminium be powder coated?

Yes. HyperFab powder-coats steel, iron, aluminium and other metals. On aluminium, a chromate (Alodine) base improves paint adhesion and corrosion resistance.

### What limits the size of a part for powder coating?

The size of the oven and spray booth, the hanging capacity and the part's weight. Heavy, thick parts also take longer to reach curing temperature. For large parts and frames, give the dimensions and weight before ordering so feasibility can be checked.

# How Sheet and Tube Punching Cost Is Determined

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/punching-cost-sheet-tube-pe-pipe/
Updated: 2026-11-15

Sheet and tube punching is priced in two parts: a one-off cost to design and build the punching die, and a cost per stroke in production. The die cost depends on geometry, hole and slot count and required accuracy; the stroke cost on material, thickness, strokes per part and quantity. Larger runs shrink the die’s share of each part.

## Short answer: what makes up the price of punching?

Punching makes holes, slots and shaped cut-outs in sheet and tube with a press stroke and a die. Because each part reaches its final shape in one or a few strokes, the price is not worked out from cut length the way laser cutting is. It has two separate parts instead: a die that is built once, and strokes that repeat throughout production.

HyperFab reviews the drawing, designs and builds a punching die for the material and thickness, punches a trial sample for your approval, and carries production and quality control through to delivery. The die cost and the cost per stroke are quoted separately after the drawing is reviewed. If HyperFab supplies the sheet or tube, material is added at current prices.

## Die cost vs cost per stroke: what is the difference?

The two costs behave differently. The die is built once and its cost is spread across the whole run, while the stroke cost repeats with every part. On a short run the die dominates the price of each part; on a long run, strokes and material take over.

In practice, anything that simplifies the die pays off most on small quantities, and anything that cuts the number of strokes per part pays off most on large ones.

|  | Punching die | Cost per stroke |
|---|---|---|
| Type of cost | One-off, before production starts | Recurring, for every stroke in production |
| Main driver | Geometry, number of holes and slots, required accuracy | Material, thickness and strokes needed per part |
| Kind of job | Simple, progressive or tube-specific die | Sheet or tube, metal or polymer |
| Effect of quantity | Share per part falls as the run grows | Repeats with every part; also depends on run quantity |
| What reduces it | Standardising hole sizes and simplifying geometry | Fewer strokes per part and a larger run |

## Punching or laser cutting: which is cheaper for your quantity?

Laser cutting needs no die, so it is cheaper for low quantities, prototypes and designs that are still changing. HyperFab’s metal laser cutting is an online service: upload a DXF file on hyperfab.ir and the price estimator quotes it instantly.

Punching is built for repeat runs with a fixed hole pattern. Once the die exists, each part is made faster and cheaper in one or a few strokes, and every part comes out the same. HyperFab offers both and recommends the right one for your quantity and geometry.

- Low quantity, a prototype or a design that is not final yet: laser cutting.
- Repeat runs with a fixed hole pattern: punching.
- Holes and slots in tube, profile or polyethylene pipe: punching with a tube-specific die.
- Somewhere in between: compare the online laser price with a punching quote for the same quantity.

## How is tube and profile punching different from sheet?

Sheet lies flat and is fully supported on the die. Tube is round and hollow, and its wall deforms under the stroke. Tube and profile punching therefore usually needs a tube-specific die that holds the section in shape during the stroke, which is one reason a tube die is priced differently from a simple sheet die.

HyperFab punches holes and slots in metal tube and profile for structures, fittings, shelving, railings and furniture. On a tube drawing, give the hole positions relative to the tube end and to each other, and their orientation around the circumference, as well as the hole shape. All of these feed directly into the die design.

## How is polyethylene (PE) pipe punched?

Punching polymer pipe is one of the harder jobs in this field. The pipe is round, the wall deforms under the stroke, and polyethylene behaves very differently from metal, so a die that works well on steel is not automatically right for PE.

HyperFab’s team has punched kidney-shaped slots in polyethylene pipe with a 125 mm diameter, 5 mm wall and 6-bar pressure rating. In another industrial project, the team was responsible for quality control of 8,000 punched tubes. Typical uses are drainage, filter, and water and air distribution pipes.

For a PE pipe quote, give the pipe diameter, wall thickness and pressure rating, the slot or hole shape, how it repeats along the length and around the circumference, and the quantity. A trial sample is punched before production so you can check the slots on the real pipe and approve them.

## How to lower punching cost: design tips before the die is built

The die is the most expensive part of the project, and most savings are made before it is built. HyperFab reviews every design from the die’s point of view, and you can get ahead of that review with a few rules:

- Keep holes a sensible distance from the edge; a hole too close to the edge distorts it under the stroke.
- Size holes in proportion to the material thickness; a hole that is very small for the thickness puts heavy load on the punch.
- Standardise hole sizes and shapes where you can; every new shape means another punch and a more complex die.
- Put tight tolerances on functional dimensions only.
- Freeze the design before the die is built; while you are still testing, make samples by laser cutting.
- State the total quantity up front so the die cost is spread over the real number of parts.

## What to send for a punching quote, and what drives the price

Send a drawing or a physical sample, the material and thickness, and an approximate quantity, or describe them by phone. For tube, add the diameter, wall thickness and hole positions along the length and around the circumference. HyperFab is based in Tehran and ships punched parts across Iran. The final price comes from the combination of the factors below, and no meaningful figure can be given before the drawing is reviewed.

- Geometry, and the number and shape of holes and slots.
- Die type: simple, progressive or tube-specific.
- Required accuracy of dimensions and hole positions.
- Material and thickness: mild steel, galvanised, stainless steel, aluminium or polymers such as polyethylene.
- Strokes needed per part, and run quantity.
- Whether HyperFab or the customer supplies the material.
- Follow-on work such as powder coating the punched parts.

For an exact quote on a punching project, call HyperFab’s industrial projects specialist on 09962233898 (+98 996 223 3898) or send the drawing on Bale. If the part can also be laser cut, you can get that price instantly on hyperfab.ir.

## FAQ

### Who owns the punching die?

The die is designed and built for your part, and its cost is quoted once, separately from the cost per stroke. Agree ownership, storage and reuse of the die for later orders with HyperFab when you receive the quotation.

### Is there a minimum quantity for punching?

Punching needs a die, so it suits repeat quantities; for low quantities, laser cutting is usually cheaper because there is no die cost. HyperFab recommends the right process for your quantity and geometry.

### Can polyethylene pipe be punched cleanly?

Yes, provided the die is designed for how polyethylene behaves rather than for metal. HyperFab’s team has punched kidney-shaped slots in 125 mm PE pipe with a 5 mm wall and 6-bar rating, and a trial sample is punched for your approval before production.

### Punching or laser cutting for a few hundred parts?

It depends on the geometry and whether the order repeats: with a fixed design and repeat orders, the die cost is spread over every run and punching can pay off. For a one-off batch or a design that may change, laser cutting is usually cheaper. Get an instant laser price on hyperfab.ir and compare it with a punching quote.

# TIG vs MIG Welding for Stainless Steel and 6000-Series Aluminium

URL: https://hyperfabgroup.github.io/en/guides/tig-vs-mig-stainless-aluminium/
Updated: 2026-11-15

TIG welding uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with filler added separately, giving clean, precise, spatter-free welds that suit thin sheet, medical equipment and cosmetic parts. MIG feeds wire continuously, so it is faster and cheaper on long structural seams. The right choice depends on material, thickness, required finish and the weld tests your project specifies.

## What is the difference between TIG and MIG welding?

The short answer: TIG is slower but more controllable and leaves a clean, even bead; MIG is faster and cheaper on long and structural welds. Neither is better across the board. Material, thickness, joint type and any cosmetic or hygiene requirements decide which one fits.

A note on names, since Iranian suppliers use Persian trade terms: “argon welding” usually means TIG, while “CO2 welding” means continuous-wire welding, the MIG/MAG family. Strictly, MIG uses an inert shielding gas such as argon and is the wire process for aluminium; with an active gas such as CO2 on carbon steel, the correct name is MAG. So “CO2 welding” is really MAG, and aluminium is never welded under CO2. TIG also runs on argon, which is why both processes sometimes get called argon welding.

| Criterion | TIG (GTAW) | MIG (GMAW) |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Slower; filler rod is added by hand | Faster; wire feeds continuously through the torch |
| Appearance | Clean, even bead with no spatter | Good, with some spatter that may need cleaning up |
| Thin vs thick material | Better on thin sheet, tube and delicate joints | More economical on thicker sections and long seams |
| Distortion | Fine heat control on thin sheet, though slow travel spreads heat on long seams | Faster travel on long seams; risk of burn-through and warping on thin sheet unless well tuned |
| Welder skill | Demands more skill and two-handed coordination | Easier to learn, but machine setup is critical |
| Typical use | Medical and food equipment, stainless tube, cosmetic parts, root passes | Chassis and frames, large structures, batch work |

## What is TIG welding and where is it used?

In TIG welding (Tungsten Inert Gas, standardised as GTAW), the arc burns between a non-consumable tungsten electrode and the workpiece while argon shields the pool from the air. Filler is added separately, so the welder controls heat and deposited metal independently and has fine command of bead shape and penetration.

The result is a narrow, clean, spatter-free weld, which is why TIG is the default for thin stainless sheet and tube, cosmetic parts, root passes, and medical and food equipment. Its weakness is speed: on long seams or thick sections labour hours and cost climb quickly.

## What is MIG welding, and how does it relate to “CO2 welding”?

In MIG welding (Metal Inert Gas, standardised as GMAW), wire feeds continuously from a spool through the torch and serves as both electrode and filler. Deposition is high, so long seams fill faster and more consistently.

What separates MIG from market “CO2 welding” is the shielding gas: inert for MIG, active for MAG. Aluminium needs inert gas, and stainless is normally welded with argon-based mixtures. Pulsed MIG reduces spatter and heat input, but the bead rarely looks as even as TIG. MIG earns its place on chassis, frames, machine bodies and large structures, where speed and cost matter most.

## Welding stainless steel: heat tint, pickling and passivation

Stainless steel resists corrosion thanks to an extremely thin chromium-oxide film. Welding heat leaves straw-to-blue colours beside the seam, called heat tint. The darker the tint, the more chromium-depleted the surface beneath it and the sooner it rusts. Controlling heat input helps, and on tube and vessels the back of the joint is purged with argon (back purging).

After welding, heat tint is usually removed by pickling or mechanical means, and the surface is passivated so the protective film reforms evenly. The details depend on the grade, service environment and project specification, so they belong on the drawing or order. Tools and brushes reserved for stainless matter too, so no carbon-steel particles are left on the surface.

In medical, food and sanitary equipment, welds must be smooth, free of crevices and pores, and easy to clean so contamination has nowhere to collect; full-penetration TIG with dressed beads is the norm. HyperFab has built many units for the medical and marine industries.

## Welding 6061 and 6063 aluminium: what to watch for

Aluminium is always covered by a thin, tough oxide skin that melts at a far higher temperature than the metal underneath. If it is not broken up, the joint does not fuse properly and oxide gets trapped in the weld. That is why aluminium is TIG welded on alternating current (AC): during the electrode-positive half-cycle the arc scours away the oxide (cleaning action), and during the other half more heat goes into the work for penetration. In MIG the wire runs electrode-positive, which gives the same cleaning action. Degreasing and brushing the joint just before welding also matter, because moisture and grease are the main causes of porosity.

The 6000-series alloys, such as 6061 and 6063, owe much of their strength to heat treatment. Welding heat partly undoes it in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), leaving that band softer than the parent metal. This happens with both TIG and MIG and must be allowed for in the structural design. These alloys are also prone to hot cracking without a suitable filler, so filler selection is part of the welding procedure.

## Weld inspection: when to use VT, PT or PAUT

HyperFab carries out visual testing (VT), liquid penetrant testing (PT), phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) and other tests on request. Which one you need depends on the defect you are worried about:

Agree acceptance criteria up front too. For fusion welds in steel, including stainless, quality levels are typically specified per ISO 5817, and for arc welds in aluminium per ISO 10042; NDT personnel qualification is commonly requested per ISO 9712. If your project calls for a particular standard or quality level, state it with the drawings.

- VT (visual testing): the baseline for every weld; checks weld shape and size, surface cracks, undercut, spatter and heat tint.
- PT (liquid penetrant): reveals surface-breaking cracks and discontinuities; the usual surface method for stainless steel and aluminium, which are generally non-magnetic.
- PAUT (phased-array ultrasonics): finds internal defects such as lack of fusion, internal cracks and porosity, with a cross-sectional image of the weld; used on full-penetration and load-bearing structural joints.

## What drives the cost of TIG and MIG welding?

Structural design is the client’s, and HyperFab fabricates to your approved drawings. The drawings are first checked for manufacturability, welding sequence and distortion control, and then quoted. The main cost drivers are:

- Material: stainless steel or 6000-series aluminium
- Weld length and type, and the process; TIG is slower, MIG faster
- Structure size and fixturing; on large frames, such as a framed chassis mounted on wheels that runs on rails, flatness and alignment over long lengths drive the effort
- Cosmetic and hygiene requirements: weld dressing, back purging and heat-tint removal
- Requested tests: VT, PT, PAUT or others
- Quantity and how repeatable the work is

For an exact quote, have your drawings, material, quantity and required tests ready and call 09962233898.

## FAQ

### Which is stronger, TIG or MIG?

Neither is inherently stronger; joint strength comes from full fusion and penetration, the right filler, and freedom from defects such as porosity and lack of fusion. On 6000-series aluminium, HAZ softening limits strength whichever process is used.

### Why does aluminium need AC TIG?

Aluminium’s oxide skin melts at a far higher temperature than the metal itself. On alternating current, the electrode-positive half-cycle breaks up that oxide and the other half delivers heat and penetration; without this cleaning action, oxide is trapped in the weld.

### What does PT detect?

Liquid penetrant testing (PT) reveals cracks, pores and other discontinuities open to the surface. A dyed liquid seeps into the flaw and, once the surface is cleaned and developer applied, the indication shows. It cannot find fully internal defects; those need ultrasonic testing.

### When is PAUT needed?

When internal defects such as lack of fusion, internal cracks or porosity matter for safety or function, typically in full-penetration and load-bearing structural welds.
